speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity in connection with an order issued by the Department of Supply and Services which, beginning in April, will reduce by one half the number of Canadian libraries which currently receive Canadian publications free of charge. In practicable application, this means that the number of libraries in Saskatchewan receiving such publications will be reduced from 25 to 8; in Manitoba, from 23 to 8; and in Alberta, from 24 to 12.

Libraries facing serious financial difficulties already will be denied the supply of such information. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That the government give reconsideration to such order, for unless this is done the libraries will cease to serve the public effectively.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I direct my question to his superior, the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers.
In view of today's dollar now being at 83.75 cents, making it the softest of the soft currencies among all industrial nations, would the minister indicate if he is aware that it has now been revealed that the United States current account deficit is only one-third, relative to their size, of our current account deficit in this country? If he is aware of that hard fact, does he agree that our sad current account position is contributing heavily to the decline of our dollar?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no additional comments to offer other than the very wise ones the Minister of Finance has made in this area. He has stated categorically in this House on several occasions the policy of the government in regard to foreign exchange.
I am, of course, generally aware of the juxtaposition of the United States current account balance, and so forth. I am not
Oral Questions
sure that is the whole, or the substance of the story. There are many other factors to be brought to bear, such as our relationship, our fiscal position vis-a-vis the provinces, the United States government's position vis-a-vis their states. All those kinds of things should be brought into context to make an objective analysis of this situation.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Having had those few words from the minister, perhaps I can go even to his superior, the emperor, the Prime Minister himself.
Bearing in mind that the Canadian dollar is now, in 1979, at the lowest level it has been in relation to the United States dollar for literally over 120 years, and bearing in mind that Mr. McNess, a well-respected economist, referring to Canada stated as follows-
I estimate that current and past devaluation is adding something in the order of an additional 4 per cent to the inflation rate-
-would the Prime Minister confirm if it is his understanding that the 83-cent dollar has cost us 4 per cent in inflation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not confirm or deny the 4 per cent, as I have not made the calculation. It is obvious, however, that a lower value to the Canadian dollar means that Canadians have to pay more for imported goods. That is the way the dollar works.
It means, therefore, that the cost of living in respect of imported items in Canada is higher than if the dollar were at par. This is the incentive to Canadians to buy things made in Canada which will create jobs for Canadians. That is how the lower value of the dollar is working, to create jobs in Canada.

A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, to the Prime Minister. Another effect of the falling dollar and the government's desperate attempts to prevent it falling further is rising interest rates.
As we learn from the United States that it is likely their rates will continue going up, and it is estimated by some economists in New York that they may be up by a point and a half in terms of United States short-term rates by next June, would the Prime Minister indicate if he intends to continue to instruct the Bank of Canada to keep raising interest rates in Canada in order to keep ahead of United States rates, notwithstanding the devastating effect high interest rates are having in this country?

I have never given any such instructions, Mr. Speaker, so I would not be called upon to give them again. As to what happens after something hypothetical or speculative occurs in the United States, the very nature of the question is out of order, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF WAGE SETTLEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. As a result of meetings with business leaders which he held over the weekend, I would like to ask whether the Prime Minister or the business leaders were able to isolate any instances of exorbitant or inflationary wage increases.
As every member of parliament knows, the industrial composite index of wage and salary increases went up only 6.4 per cent, which was less than the increase in the cost of living. If the Prime Minister has any information in this respect, would he tell the House who these groups are?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF WAGE SETTLEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were several instances referred to of settlements which were considerably above the average figure mentioned by the hon. member-a figure of 6 per cent to 7 per cent.
Concern was expressed that these increasing rates of settlement might lead to double-digit inflation if Canadians were trying to compensate themselves for increased costs of goods imported from abroad, whether it be increased costs of energy because of the rise dictated by the OPEC nations, or whether it be increased costs of goods imported with the Canadian dollar worth less than it had been in the previous year. These instances were referred to. There was no general consensus that we would go into double-digit inflation; on the contrary, the hope was expressed that some of these settlements would, by their nature, be catch-up and would not indicate a trend. The hope was that the trend would continue to show the restraint that was shown in the past year by union and management.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the President of the Treasury Board: it deals with classification.
Might I remind him that a complete audit, a report as of December 1 back in 1976, indicated there was good evidence that the administration of the classification system was deteriorating? Since the government has stated its intention to introduce Bill C-12 which has to do with indexation, a related matter, when are we to be told what the answers are to this serious problem of overclassification which, I say, is costing the Canadian people some $75 million a year: I dispute the minister's estimate that it is costing $45 million? Why the foot-dragging after all these years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF OVERCLASSIFICATION OF POSITIONS
speechtext:
Again, Mr. Speaker, I take issue with the figure of $75 million. I took the same position when replying to one of the hon. member's colleagues. I said at the time that even taking into account a degree of indexation, we felt the maximum figure would be $50 million. Even so, that is a lot of money and the position is still very far from satisfactory as far as we are concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: GRAIN DUST
speechtext: Has grain dust been suspected as a possible cause of grain elevator explosions and does it have a nutritional value comparable to the whole grain from which it is generated and, if so, is the government considering the possibility of compacting grain dust for handling as a potential ingredient in livestock feed?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: GRAIN DUST
speechtext:
Grain dust is suspected as a possible cause of grain elevator explosions. It becomes ignitable when a combination of critical conditions are met. The known critical factors under which dust will explode with damaging force are high temperature at source of ignition, concentration of dust in suspension, size of dust particles and moisture content of the dust particles. When ignition occurs within a confined space, it may cause an explosion.
Grain dust is considered to have good nutritional value for livestock, although not necessarily as highly nutritious as the whole grain from which it is generated. Such dust captured by dust collection systems in terminal elevators, together with other refuse screenings from the cleaning systems, is lightweight material which is bulky and difficult to transport. In order to overcome this problem, it can be concentrated by pelleting into livestock feed. Almost all grain process elevators in Canada have pellet mills as an integral part of their terminal operations, concentrating this by-product and exporting it as grain screenings pellets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of those who have participated in the debate on this bill have said that this piece of legislation is one of the most important ever to be discussed in this parliament. I agree with those sentiments wholeheartedly. It has even been acknowledged by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). To show the urgency and gravity of this legislation, a view shared by all sides of the House, I would like to quote from the hon. member's speech. Before I read from it, however, I should say that this will probably be the only time in this debate that I will agree with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. She said:
This is one of the most important, one of the most major, bills ever to come before the Canadian parliament, because by its very nature it has tremendous bearing on our established political process. This bill gives to the governor in council, the cabinet, the executive, power to initiate referenda on constitutional matters. Nothing could be more substantive or more serious. It is serious not just because of its constitutional aspects, with which I shall deal in a few minutes, but it is doubly serious because a referendum of any kind at the national level is a serious matter in itself.
I completely agree with those statements. Then, however, the hon. member and her colleagues went on to attack Bill C-9 in a most ferocious way.
I was not here on Friday, but 1 had the benefit of watching the CBC program "This Week in Parliament" last night, and when I saw some of the histrionics which went on in this Chamber on Friday-especially by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro)-I was astonished. I believe he said that he was appalled; but I was appalled that he would drag the debate on this bill down to the level which he did. I will let the hon. member's words and actions speak for themselves. They are on videotape, and anyone can see them if they wish.
The Conservative party attacked this bill as undermining responsible government, speaking of course in the context of British parliamentary democracy. This in itself is a valid concern and I have no quarrel with it. In the first part of my remarks this afternoon I will deal with this concern, but from a

The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) also spoke on this bill on November 12. He gave the classic, responsible government defence, and so he should since he is a former professor of philosophy. Although the hon. member did not quote him by name, which would be anathema to him, he really gave the defence, if you will, of the Edmund Burke thesis of the fiduciary role of an elected representative. That is a person elected to use his or her judgment over a particular period, a representative not subject to the whim of instant recall or of his or her constitutents, but a representative who must account for his or her actions at election time.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby eloquently summed up the arguments. I would like those hon. members of the Conservative party who are present to hear the rest of his remarks. At page 2043 of Hansard for December 12, 1978, he said:
Democracy should be concerned with electing men and women to study issues seriously, to recognize the complexity of most problems and to work out a fair solution.
He went on to say that the problems facing us now and the problems posed to this country by the introduction of a referendum in the province of Quebec mean that we should go beyond the traditional role of parliamentary democracy, the traditional attitude that Edmund Burke had and what he felt about the role of the member of parliament. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby went on to plead that the special case of the proposed referendum in Quebec gives parliament no choice but to provide itself with a means to consult all of the people.
I wish to develop this argument further than the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby did in order to counter the proposition put forward by the Tories. Perhaps it is quite academic and it might be too philosophical, but I think we are dealing with a matter of fundamental importance and that we should look at the philosophical aspects of the debate very closely.
As one who was born and raised in Great Britain and in my early years schooled in the magnificent fairness of the British parliamentary system, I have only the utmost respect for the monarchy, for British parliamentary institutions and our system of common law. The Conservative party should realize, however, that not only do societies evolve as time goes by but the laws that govern society also evolve.
That is what is happening in Canada today. Canada is no longer a British dominion. I hate to bring this matter to the attention of hon. members opposite, but it is no longer a British dominion. We have inherited the monarchy and we have inherited common law and parliament, and I am glad we have, Mr. Speaker. But our society itself has changed radically since the war, so radically that the proportion of those who had ancestry in the British Isles has fallen to about 40 per cent of our population. One or two per cent of the population are native people, about 27 per cent have French ancestry and the

balance of around 30 per cent comes from varying backgrounds. There are many of these people in this House, and many on the other side.
These people have not always been touched by responsible government in the British context. Those of non-British stock do not necessarily appreciate or accept the rather nebulous British constitutional system of guarantees for basic liberties- a system composed of laws passed by parliament, customs and judicial decisions. A great body of opinion in Canada today does not accept the supremacy of parliament to protect rights. In fact, even the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) agrees with that, because in 1959-60 he introduced the Canadian Bill of Rights to protect individual liberties. He knew how important it was. The trouble is that the Canadian Bill of Rights does not stand up. It is not good enough. We need these rights basically entrenched. I wonder what the right hon. member for Prince Albert would say on this particular matter.
The British constitution is an oddity in a world of codified constitutions. For example, those who came to Canada from continental Europe, like our neighbours in the United States, innately feel that constitutional guarantees are best safeguarded by codification rather than by legislative action. It must be acknowledged that the British constitution approach which believes in the supremacy of parliament is stoutly defended in English speaking Canada-and often emotionally. At the recent constitutional conference, for example, it was Premier Lyon of Manitoba who vigorously defended the supremacy of legislative action as the ultimate safeguard for basic rights. This is a particular point of view that Premier Lyon and others are entitled to.
This proposition was also defended last summer in the deliberations of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution. Some members of the Senate on our side and on the other side defended that approach. Indeed, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield)-who I am glad to see in the House today during my speech-made the same point in committee. There is nothing wrong with it, Mr. Speaker. My question is whether this particular point is applicable in Canada in the present context.
The classic "responsible government" approach is becoming tougher to defend in twentieth century society, not only in Canada but also in Great Britain. Those who are quick to bark on the other side should look at what is happening on the other side of the pond in relation to what is happening to responsible government, aside from all their labour troubles. They should pay attention to what is happening in a constitutional sense in Great Britain, the mother of parliamentary democracy.
Let us look at this country for a moment, Mr. Speaker. Over the past century we have seen responsible government safeguard rights-to use Mr. Lyon's terminology-by the 1890 act of the Manitoba legislature which rendered inoperative the institutional bilingualism provisions in section 23 of the Manitoba act. In 1912 there was the promulgation of the infamous regulation 17 in the province of Ontario which made English the sole language of that province. This parliament
January 29, 1979

cannot be absolved from not protecting the rights of individuals. The internment of Japanese Canadians in World War I! resulted from the application of section 3 of the War Measures Act, passed in 1940.
I am saying that perhaps legislatures are not the best guarantors of individual liberties. 1 am challenging this traditional argument that is supported not only by Premier Lyon but by his Conservative minions or his colleagues in this House.
There are some elements of Bill 101 that are an infringement on the rights of the minority. I am sure hon. members opposite have supported the challenges made in the Supreme Court of Canada of those sections of Bill 101. So much, Mr. Speaker, for legislative protection of minority rights.
We now consider Quebec's referendum which will ask for some consensus on sovereignty association or independence where presumably the unconstitutional provisions of Bill 101 would be enshrined in law. Who is to stop that particular referendum? No one, Mr. Speaker, because it is well within the ambit of provincial legislatures, provincial governments and the provinces to hold a referendum on any issue. It does not apparently strike one as logical, however, nor does it strike one as being fair or responsible, that the parliament of Canada should also have the tool of the referendum to counter any referendum that takes place in a province where the question has not been put fairly or there is some question as to the accuracy of the result of that particular referendum. 1 say it is logical, it is fair and it is responsible.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) who has been heckling me throughout my speech should read some of the speeches of his leader. He is at odds with his leader. He should do his homework if he does not agree with the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. That party supports Bill C-9.

Even in the mother of parliaments there has been a question of whether or not basic rights are being guaranteed by parliament itself.
In March a referendum will be held in Great Britain on the question of devolution of powers to Wales and Scotland. So much for our great British parliamentary tradition. Even in Great Britain they are recognizing British parliamentary democracy must change, must evolve, and must adapt to changing circumstances.
The Conservative party attacks Bill C-9 using arguments either outdated or that have failed both in Canada and in the United Kingdom. How else is one to decide whether to entrench rights or not to entrench rights, to devolve power or concentrate power? How else are we to decide that? Partisan politics often obscure the real issues in constitutional debate. We have seen it in this House with reference to Bill C-9 and we saw it at the special joint committee last fall when the official opposition were not serious about trying to find new ways to devise a constitution for this country. My answer is provided right here in Bill C-9. The people collectively should be the ones that are consulted on basic constitutional changes.
The Tories say "no" for consulting the people by means of a referendum; or if you want to use another phrase, by direct democracy. January 29, 1979

issue No. 1 of the special joint committee minutes for August 15, 1978:
The attitude of the provinces makes one pause and think and is also an eloquent expression of the kind of attitudes which are now prevalent. You say that you are going to consult with people, but I think it would be more important to consult the provincial representatives of the people of Canada. It is all fine and well to speak directly to the people, but if you go over the heads of the 10 provincial governments, you are going to have trouble.
Trouble from whom? You will have trouble from the Canadian people who are sick and tired of the games the Conservative party play on constitutional reform and in debate on this bill. Their view of democracy is to get together and make deals with the provincial premiers. They do not want to consult the people.
At least the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands is consistent. Her view is: "The hell with the people, we will just look at the views of the provincial governments". The Conservative party has come up with a view very much akin to the Bundesrat in Germany. That is a form of upper house bringing the provincial governments into the centre. This view was also expressed by the Task Force on National Unity and the Ontario task force. That is one way of looking at it. I do not think it is the way Canadians want to deal with constitutional reform.
Let us go to another quote from the deliberations of that committee. This is Professor Edward McWhinney, head of political science at Simon Fraser university, a very eminent individual who has travelled all over the world. What does Professor McWhinney say on this matter? He is talking about the Bundesrat hang-up. I do not think he said hang-up; that is my word. Referring to the Bundesrat, he said:
-it is basically a conclave of princely rulers meeting for executive purposes, and the analogy with our Senate or the attempt to make an analogy with the Senate I think is misplaced. The better analogy would be to the federal-provincial conferences-
I share that view of Professor McWhinney. The Bundesrat may have been applicable in the nineteenth century or postwar Germany because of the very nature of the German state and the way the German principalities and states came together to form modern Germany, but that is not the answer for Canada today. I completely oppose any view of a Bundesrat approach being sneaked into the parliament of Canada.
I want to deal further with this basic argument on the Bundesrat and who speaks for Canada. In fact, I think the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands used those words. We know the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has used them. They have become a sort of password-Who is speaking for Canada? I say the people should speak for Canada. The hon. member and her colleagues say the provincial governments should speak for Canada?
I have been elected to represent a particular constituency in metropolitan Toronto. There are provincial members in that constituency. One of them recently made a statement criticizing the federal government. That is fine; in the context of our British parliamentary tradition it is fair ball for provincial ministers continually to hammer away at Ottawa. However, it seems that federal ministers and members should not attack

the provinces. That is not considered fair. As far as I am concerned, I have as much right to speak in this chamber and throughout the land on matters affecting municipal or provincial jurisdictions as have my provincial and municipal counterparts to speak about federal matters.
This view obviously is not shared by members opposite. What they really want is a confederationist approach in the classical mould. They want to bring the provincial governments into the Senate chamber, the upper house. They want them to have veto power over legislation passed by this House.
In Bill C-60 introduced in the last session was a very novel and ingenious way of bringing the regions into the centre. Bill C-60 proposed a form of proportional representation in the Senate where the parties in the legislatures-not just the government party but all of the parties in each legislature, whether it be the PQ in Quebec, the Liberals in Ontario or whatever-would have the opportunity to represent their legislatures. Half would be appointed by the provincial parties and half by the federal government. That would bring in an element of proportional representation.
There was a delaying power in the proposed Bill C-60. However, the Conservatives did not want that. They regard the true voice of the people as being in Queen's Park or the Grande Allee. That is not true. We are the true repository of what Canadians think.

What is one to do? If we want a new dream or a new vision for Canada, if we want to resurrect the spirit of 1864, even in the absence of any consensus on the part of the provinces and the federal government, we should consult with the people. However, the Tories do not want that. They disagree with it.
I see my time is running out. I am sure members opposite will be glad because I have said a few things they did not want to hear. The truth really hurts them. I will conclude by again quoting Professor McWhinney when talking about constitutional reform in general terms. This was said on the same day, September 26, I quote:
The key is popular consensus. If you draft a constitution without popular consensus it may be what Mr. Justice Owen Roberts of the United States Supreme Court called "a railway excursion ticket, good for one journey on one train at one particular time to one particular place." ... So I stress this issue of a prior societal consensus as a fundamental condition of successful constitutional making.
That is what Bill C-9 is all about. We want to get society's consensus on the direction in which we should move. Members opposite argue that our party does not really know what this

I want to deal for a moment with the suggestion that this is merely a consultative mechanism before us as proposed in the government's Bill C-9. I do not wish to dwell on this at any great length; I simply want to quote the words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde). There is a danger in pretending that we can ignore the advice that is given on referenda. If we adopt holus-bolus what is proposed in the bill, the practice of referenda on practically every subject-that is what the government is proposing here-we will create a situation wherein the ability of parliament to do what parliament was established to do, to do what Edmund Burke described as the role of parliament-to cast our judgment and then be held accountable for it at elections-will be severely circumscribed.
I quote no better an authority-and I rarely quote him as an authority-than the Minister of Justice himself. He said in answer to a question by my hon. friend from Grenville-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker) on December 12:
If the government does not proceed to do anything about it surely the people of Canada would ask themselves why they had to go through with that exercise in the first place.
Exactly. Of course that question would be asked, particularly if we had more and more recourse to referenda. There would be increasing pressure on the part of the people who were consulted and saw their views ignored not to have their views ignored. There would be a continuing attrition of the fundamental and traditional role-not simply in other countries but in this country-of the House of Commons.
The other matter the Minister of Justice referred to was also said in answer to a question. It was not a prepared remark but it may well be one of great significance. He said:
There is nothing in the constitution at the present time which could make the result of a referendum binding on the government, parliament or any particular legislature.
I am not sure what he meant by the phrase "at the present time" but I think it is a phrase we all have to consider when we ask ourselves exactly what the intentions of the government are with regard to this legislation it is introducing.
The circumstances under which this bill has been put forward in parliament and the unmistakable implications of the language of the legislation are such that hon. members of this House will have to consider our responsibilities with even more
Referenda
than our usual seriousness. As has been said by almost every speaker here, this is an unusually important piece of legislation. It is important because, while the bill is very innocent in what it pretends to do, it is very dangerous in what it proposes to do.
As hon. members will recall, the matter arose as a relatively modest proposal relating to the fairness of the proposed referendum in the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston), who is in his place today, spoke on Friday. I regret that I was not here; I was meeting with the man who hopes to replace him. The hon. member indicated that it was his view that this power would never be used. That is an interesting view, and I rather regret that the hon. member for Westmount did not have an opportunity, to elaborate on why he thought it would not be used, either in the specific application of which he was speaking or, more dangerously, in the much larger application of which this bill is possible. This bill would allow federal referenda on literally every question under the sun. That is what the legislation provides.
When the modest proposal arose, it arose in the context of the proposal in the fall of 1977 by the government of Quebec when it released its white paper on referenda which was in anticipation of the provincial referendum legislation which came forward later, in December of 1977. Certain of the ground rules which were set out in the Quebec white paper were felt to place severe and undue restrictions on traditional freedom of association and expression in a political compaign. As a result, there was very serious fear in the province of Quebec, a very serious negative reaction and a very serious view across the country that it was not going to be possible to have some of our traditional liberties safeguarded in the conduct of this referendum campaign.
At about that same time-and I am sure there was some relationship between the two events-the Prime Minister began to make suggestions about the need to provide the federal government with what he called at that time the same tools as the Parti Quebecois government had. In his annual New Year's interview on CTV, the Prime Minister explained the role he anticipated referendum legislation at the federal level would play. I think it is useful to place on the record the words the Prime Minister used at that time. This was at Christmas, 1977:
You could use it in Quebec to contradict or double check an erroneous or undemocratic Quebec referendum. You could use it in the other nine provinces after Quebec would have hypothetically voted to a question: "Are you in favour of independence and association", and if the answer is yes, then you ask the rest of Canada ... I don't want to put the referendum as the centerpiece of our action. It is purely a counteroffensive tool.
That was what the Prime Minister said in 1977, and that is the reason for our concern. That description is dramatically different from what is in fact proposed in the bill before us. The Prime Minister went on at that time to say that a referendum-and I quote:
-is not something which is in the nature of a parliamentary system.
I recommend that to his acolyte from York East. I want to return to that theme later on, but for the moment it is

important to remember that the first proposal was to provide the Government of Canada with what the Prime Minister called a counteroffensive tool in the event that the province of Quebec rigged the question or rigged the rules of the referendum it was having. This proposed counteroffensive tool was said to be needed in the event that the national government needed a referendum or an instrument to answer an initiative which was taken by referendum in the province of Quebec. It was to be counteroffensive, and it was limited at that time to one circumstance and to one circumstance only.
Among the advantages of that modest, limited proposal at that time was that it fell within the Canadian tradition of the limited use of referenda. When we have referenda before, they have always dealt with specific questions which were always clearly within the jurisdiction of the sponsoring government, and the authority sought of parliament was always limited and specific as to a particular question. Even though that tradition has not contributed at all to national unity or the national harmony of the country, that is none the less the tradition which exists; and if the government wants to proceed within the Canadian tradition, it need only come to parliament with a bill providing for a specific referendum on a particular question. There would certainly be widespread support in this House for a specific Canadian referendum ensuring the fairness of the question put regarding the future of the province of Quebec. If that is what the government wanted, that is what it should have asked for. Instead, it is asking for something very different and which is very dangerous to the country.

I should like to deal with the language of the legislation, which I am afraid some government members have overlooked. It draws a much broader sweep than their remarks seem to indicate. The referendum power is to deal with the constitution of Canada which, according to clause 2 of the legislation, the definition clause-
-includes, without limiting the meaning of that expression,
(a)	the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of Canada, and
(b)	the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada-
One must think for a minute what that means. Or better yet, I challenge anyone in the House to try to think of some Canadian question which is not embraced by that wide definition. The definition allows the government to have a referendum on anything it wants.
What does it mean in practice? Let us look at the language. What is a custom in Canada? What is a convention within the Canadian system? I will not give an exhaustive list because it would take the rest of my life, but I should like to refer to
Referenda
some examples. Cabinet government is a custom or a convention in the country. Are we to have referenda on cabinet government? Ministerial responsibility is or has been a custom or convention in the country. Is there to be a national referendum on ministerial responsibility? I hesitate to raise the subject of the monarchy because members opposite are so sensitive on the question, but the monarchy is a convention in the Canadian constitution. Is there to be a referendum on the monarchy? Federal-provincial conferences are a convention in the Canadian constitution. Are we to have a yes or no referendum on federal-provincial conferences? In fact, the parliamentary system is a custom which is not written into law. Does the government intend to have a national yes or no referendum on the parliamentary system? The power to do so is in the bill. That is what the government is requesting: the power to have referenda on the monarchy, on cabinet government, on ministerial responsibility and on a number of other things.
The fundamental rule of law in this country is a custom. Is it to be put to referendum? The bill asks for the power to put that question to referendum. What are enactments? The referendum power has to do with enactments. Let me cite a few examples. One of them is the Canadian Bill of Rights; another is the Indian Act. The Supreme Court of Canada draws its existence from an enactment, as does the right to vote. Is the right to vote to be the subject of a referendum? Because the bill permits the government to ask for a referendum on that question.
What about political and judicial institutions and processes? What does that include? Among other things it includes a free press, the party system and the distribution of powers among different levels of government. Are those to be the subject of referenda? That is the power which the government is requesting in Bill C-9. For example, they are asking for the power to put the question of freedom of the press to referendum.
I do not accuse the government of proposing referenda on these subjects specifically. I suspect its reason for widening the power it seeks is much more precise. The government wants a weapon it can use against any province in the event of disagreement about a particular constitutional reform. Perhaps it will be patriation, perhaps it will be natural resources. Hon. members of the New Democratic Party, given the interest of their last remaining premier on the question of provincial jurisdiction over natural resources, might want to take a look at whether they are so enthusiastic about this bill which would empower the government and all governments to have national referenda on whether Saskatchewan should surrender its jurisdiction over natural resources.
Perhaps it will be on some other question that the government would seek to pressure a province with a yes or a no answer on a complex question. As I will argue later, even that is dangerous and counterproductive. The power being requested in this bill goes well beyond that. As members of parliament, it is incumbent upon us to have an obligation to do more than consult. Also we have an obligation to protect particularly the rights of minorities and others who might be injured by

I do not at all question the government's motives, but I think the government has been wrong in its analysis of this nation, and wrong in its approach to unity in this nation. One of the reasons we are so divided now is that the central government has been wrong and stubborn on key questions. As more than one observer has pointed out, the Pepin-Robarts task force report amounts to a repudiation of many elements of the government's approach and many elements of the government's stewardship. Uniting this nation requires much more than having a means to try to force the premiers into line. On key questions like the integrity and unity of this nation there can be no negotiation, none at all. On other questions, including distribution of powers and patriation, there can be real progress only with real agreement, and that kind of real agreement requires an atmosphere of co-operation.
We have made some progress in constitutional talks lately. I must say we have made particular progress since the government discovered and adopted the recommendations of the Kingston conference. It would be tragic if that atmosphere of progress, minor and recent, were destroyed by Ottawa using the weapon it is seeking today to blackmail the provinces into accepting unacceptable constitutional changes. That, sir, would recreate the confrontation that has done so much damage to this country.
[ Translation\
Mr. Speaker, I believe we should put aside the case of Quebec for a moment because as concerns the issue of constitutional referenda, Quebec is in a special situation since it will have its own referendum to determine its constitutional future. Naturally, the Canadian government needs special powers to hold its own referendum in Quebec on this same issue. Everyone agrees about this. There have already been cases in Canada where the federal government was empowered to hold a referendum on a specific issue when necessary. And we can face the particular problem involving the situation in Quebec by using the same methods that have been implemented in our Canadian traditions.
However, this bill makes important changes in the way of using referenda in Canada. This bill grants much more power to the federal government and allows it to ask questions related to constitutional matters under provincial jurisdiction. When he introduced this bill, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) said that this tool could be used if the process of constitutional review breaks down. In other words, Ottawa could use a referendum in the case of what the minister has called a constitutional review breakdown. This bill will allow Ottawa to ask the opinion of the public throughout Canada to attempt to force any province to accept constitution? 1 changes with which it disagrees. We can now think of instances where this power could be used to the detriment of one province or another. The federal government could use this tool to attack Saskatchewan in relation with the rights of this province as concerns natural resources. It could also attack the jurisdiction
Referenda
of Quebec in educational matters, for instance. It could attack the jurisdiction of coastal provinces as concerns offshore resources.
This means that this new power in the hands of Ottawa will certainly cause new tensions in the area of federal-provincial relations. It is totally in the spirit of confrontation that prevails within the federal government every time it must deal with the provinces. A national government convinced that progress is possible through co-operation rather than confrontation would not ask for such a tool which proves useful only when there is disagreement. The mere fact that it requires such a tool shows that Ottawa is expecting even more confrontation with the provinces. Such a presumption is quite dangerous because if one starts discussions while expecting disagreement, there is bound to be disagreement.
If we really want to make progress, we must take an entirely different approach to federal-provincial relations. We must recognize that the only way to renew the Canadian federalism is to reach a consensus among all governments. Blackmail is not an answer. The only solution is to agree. For some years, the premiers of provinces other than Quebec have seemed increasingly willing to consider reforms that would ensure the development of the Quebec culture within a renewed federalism. English Canada is favourable to change, and it is most important for the cause of federalism in Quebec that the national government be in a position to work in consultation with the provinces that want reforms instead of fighting with all the provinces.
The essence of my intervention in this debate is quite simple, and I repeat it now. If the government feel that a referendum on a specific question is necessary, then let them come and put it to this House of Commons. Let them do it in the Canadian way and ask a specific question, not seek this immense power which would allow the national government to run referenda on virtually any question. If it would like that kind of support, then let them come to this House of Commons and ask for it. But we say "no" to this bill that demands so much excessive power.
If the government came forward and asked us for what they say they want, then they would get a different hearing; but they are asking for something much more. They are asking for a power that is dangerous in the hands of this or any government. That is a power which we in this parliament, being conscious of our traditions, of the need to protect minorities and others who might be abused by the power, of the fact that the only way in which we will get agreement and progress in this nation is for different governments to agree and come together, knowing that you do not get agreement by blackmail, will resist, as this bill is written now. It is an attempt to grab more power than is needed for purposes which are not stated by this government.

The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) called upon the Speaker to declare that the words "deliberate distortion" were unparliamentary and requested withdrawal by the member who made the comment. The Speaker of the day said:
Order, please. As the hon. member knows much better than I, there are a number of precedents and a number of authors who list long series of words considered to be unparliamentary. Basically I would think the suggestion by a member that there has been a deliberate intention to mislead the House is normally not acceptable according to the practices of this House. Although the hon. member may have wanted to say there had been a distortion, I am quite sure he did not want to impute to any hon. member an intention to deliberately distort something. I should like that hon. member to confirm my understanding of this situation.
The speaker required withdrawal. The second precedent occurred on May 26, 1972 at page 2589 of Hansard and is also cited on the relevant page of Beauchesne. At the foot of the page with respect to the remarks made by the then member for Skeena, the Speaker intervened, called for order and said:
The hon. member knows that another member should not be accused of deliberately distorting what has been said. He can say that it has been distorted, but he has no right to say the distortion was deliberate.
On that occasion as well the offensive words uttered by the member at the time had to be withdrawn.
I suggest, since the hon. member for York East is now in his seat, that the gentlemanly thing for him to do in the face of those precedents is to rise and, if not apologize for the use of that unparliamentary term, at least have the good grace to withdraw it.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this debate on second reading and referral to committee of Bill C-9 that would empower the Parliament of Canada to hold referenda on constitutional matters.

Before I go into my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to deal briefly with the tone and content of the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I wonder if the leader of the Opposition has read the bill, because in his attempt to attack and blur the government's position on the constitutional question and the national unity question, he repeatedly said in his speech that the government wants the power to hold the referendum, to do this and to do that. Section 4 and 5 of Bill C-9, at pages 6 and 7, clearly state that any proclamation or order in council to hold a referendum must be approved by this House. The bill provides for 40 hours of debate on the motion.
This House of Commons must approve this motion before a referendum can be held, so how misleading-but not deliberately of course. When a man of the stature of the leader of a national party rises in this House and bases the whole premise of his speech and his attack on the government on the fact that this government would like far-reaching powers to hold refe-rendums, I do not know what to think. He feels that it is terrible to ask this House to pass this bill because it is going too far in asking for powers to hold referendums. If the hon. member had read the bill on that 14-hour flight from Tokyo to Bangkok to India, he would have seen that the government could not hold a referendum without asking parliament to approve the motion and to provide for 40 hours of debate.
Again, it is a reflection of the Conservative party's stand on this issue to only attack the government. Quite the contrary! Did the Leader of the Opposition not hear some premiers during the last constitutional conference object to the entrenchment of language rights in the constitution? Mr. Speaker, we must also correct the imbalance which lies in the present constitution whereby under section 133 the English Canadians in Quebec have written rights in that province that French Canadians do not have in other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, our purpose is not to assess what a provincial government does or does not do for the French-speaking community in the province, be it today, next week or in six months' time. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the bill we are dealing with is one of the most important to come before the House in quite a long time. As a matter of fact, Bill C-9 is a major part of the response which the government of Canada is giving to the crisis which exists in Canada since November 15, 1976. The second part of this response is the constitutional debate which has taken a new turn following the introduction in June 1978 of a government bill dealing with constitutional amendments. The purpose of that bill was to start discussions and provoke a debate both within our parliamentary institutions and elsewhere in Canada.
This bill has truly given rise to a good debate, and I think it has compelled our politicians and encouraged all Canadians to become aware of this issue. On the day which followed the election of the Parti Quebecois in the province of Quebec, I urged the government to hold a referendum or an election, and to provide Quebeckers with a democratic means to indicate their intentions as to the future of our country. If I suggested that at the time, it was for a very simple reason. The political context of such a referendum is extremely important, I would even say crucial. I felt that obviously the PQ would stage the referendum campaign in a style that would create controversy. Well, that is exactly what has happened. That is exactly what is happening.
Mr. Speaker, I think that all Canadians, all those who wish to keep our country together should rejoice and approve a bill which asks parliament to incorporate in our statutes a legal means to hold a federal referendum on constitutional issues when the need arises, be it before, during or after the Quebec referendum. The important thing is that the situation has changed. The opposition leader speaks of British traditions, of the necessity to settle this question among politicians, among federal and provincial parliamentarians. He speaks, Mr. Speaker, naively, irresponsibly, as if the people in power in Quebec are good people, people who will put the question clearly and honestly when the referendum is held. How naive can one be! Whoever understands that Rene Levesque and the Parti Quebecois are using Quebec nationalism as a vehicle for politics, as a political tool, cannot speak that way, Mr. Speaker. Whoever understands that must be aware that Rene Levesque and the Parti Quebecois are now telling the rest of Canada: Meet our terms or we go. That is blackmail, Mr. Speaker.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) claims this government is resorting to blackmail. All of Canada is being threatened with blackmail by people who would split the country. When the Leader of the Opposition speaks of our diversity, of its strength, of the importance of respecting our diversity, I agree with him. I too appreciate the diversity of Canada, but not to the extent of destroying Canada. The
January 29, 1979

leader does not know his history, Mr. Speaker. Let him go back 3,000 years before Christ, to the days of the Sumerians and Akkadians-Akkadians with a double "k", in the country of Akkad-what destroyed those civilizations after hundreds of years, almost 1,000 years? What caused their destruction, Mr. Speaker? The lack of autonomy of their city-states. Those city-states, through which the aspirations of the people could be represented locally; those civilizations simply wanted to respect the diversity of their civilization; after 700 years, the Sumerian civilization collapsed simply because there was no central power.
Naturally, I respect the diversity of Canada, but I shall not do so when there is someone in power in one of the provinces, one of the most important in Canada, which represents about one fourth of the population in Canada, who says: I am going to use the diversity of Canada to destroy it. Mr. Speaker, that is what is going on in Quebec, and when we say we want to have a federal referendum, it is because we want to make sure that both the question and the answer, the question put by the referendum and the answer given to it by Quebeckers, are very clear, and that everyone understands them.
I must once again ask this question: Why is the Leader of the Opposition, deceiving the people on such an important matter by saying that we want the power to hold a referendum on anything he says "anything under the sun"-when the bill clearly states that it is for constitutional matters, that before holding a referendum, the government will have to go before parliament with only 40 hours of debate in the House of Commons. I wonder why the Leader of the Opposition resorts to such distortions especially in a debate as important as this one on the future of Canada. Is it because he meets people who oppose this government, only because it so happens that this government has quite simply decided 10 or 15 years ago to try and correct some historical injustices, Mr. Speaker. I wonder why the Progressive Conservative party and its leader do not come out with a clear position on this and why, when he criticizes the bill, he skirts the truth. I wonder!
As I was saying earlier, a constitutional reform is a significant element of the federal government's answer to the Quebec situation. It is indeed because even though we can say no to the government of Quebec, we cannot say no to Quebeckers. We must provide Quebeckers with an alternative, we must tell them that our political institutions in Canada can be altered so that Canada's French-speaking citizens, in Quebec and elsewhere, can really become full-fledged citizens. That is what must be done, Mr. Speaker. And I must admit that I find it difficult to control my temper because I seldom get emotional on political matters. I can play the political game, however, when we are talking about the future of the country, it is a little different. And it is hard for me not to blow up when I hear people inside and outside the House say that the government gives too much importance to the constitutional reform and national unity issues.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of drawing up a national navigation policy, the prime objective of which would be to lay a favourable groundwork for the setting up of a true Canadian merchant marine.

January 29, 1979
Merchant Marine

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for seconding this motion, as well as members on the government side who will no doubt support it.
It gives me great pleasure to submit to the House at this time this sensitive issue of a Canadian merchant marine. Over the last few years there have been significant developments in Canada in the area of transportation. As early as 1975, a national transportation policy proposal was put forth by the then minister and member for Langelier, Mr. Marchand. That was followed by the creation of VIA Rail, the passage of the Maritime Code and the coasting trade legislation. Many of us saw the Maritime Code and the coasting trade legislation as the first steps towards the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine.
However, we are now in 1979 and this has not yet materialized. Nothing concrete has been done to revive the merchant marine that we had even before the first and second world wars. Through lack of concern, our successive governments have let the situation deteriorate to such an extent that things could not be worse. We have all the human, technological and material resources at our disposal to establish a merchant marine, yet no action is being taken.
Need I remind the House that at the beginning of this century Canada's merchant fleet ranked fourth in the world? But year after year it slipped back compared to those of other industrialized countries. Of course, at that time the government did not see fit to intervene directly. By 1944, reports were submitted which showed, among other things, that the private sector was not much interested in the operation of a merchant marine and that grants were essential. Yet no positive action was taken and we started to sell our ships at the end of the last world war. In 1958 we still had a Crown corporation, the Canadian National Steamship Company, which still operated a dozen of ships, all of which were abandoned that same year. Now, 20 years later, we are still at the same point, and that is unbelievable.
I would like at this time, Mr. Speaker, to quote some figures in order to throw some light on the situation of the international maritime traffic in our waters. The most recent figures are for the month of April 1978. During that one-month period, we had 1,720 arrivals of ships carrying close to five million short tons of freight, and the same number of departures of ships carrying 8.8 million short tons of freight. The potential is there, nobody can deny it. Yet, according to an OECD study published in 1976, our country ranked last among OECD countries, on the same level as Switzerland and Germany, two countries which have no littoral. That is quite an honour, Mr. Speaker.
For instance, according to Statistics Canada, in 1976, 200 freighters were loaded in Canadian ports with goods to be shipped to the United Kingdom, and out of those 200 freight-

ers, only two were Canadian registered. It is likely that it was the same ship. The most common registration countries are Denmark, Norway, Liberia, Panama, Greece, Germany, the United Kingdom and Russia. According to the latest studies, that last country has made tremendous progress recently and is already almost monopolizing maritime traffic throughout the world. Indeed, since the last war the U.S.S.R. has increased its merchant marine threefold or fivefold, to the extent that it is now in position to assume definite control over the huge potential of transport tenders by merchant marine. Conditions are about the same for the transport of goods from the United Kingdom to Canada. 1 could also mention that in the case of Belgium and Luxemburg, of 100 ships travelling from those countries to Canada, only one alone was flying the Canadian colours and finally in the case of France, only one of 150 ships carried the Canadian flag.
In reply to question No. 79 put on the order paper by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), the Minister of Transport answered that only three ships of Canadian registry are doing some trade abroad, not taking into consideration of course the boats on the Great Lakes. In 1960, there were 18; in 1950, 88; in 1945, 173. Of our three ships, only one is anchored in Quebec City and it is the Edgar Jourdain which belongs to Mr. Jules Jourdain of Rimouski who feels rightly that the Canadian maritime policy is prejudicial to him. This man deserves our admiration because he persists in spite of everything in hoisting the Canadian flag on his ships which is one of the very few which are plying the seas around the world. Ships hoisting convenience flags in our waters are twice as numerous as they were two years ago, in spite of their low security standards. Indeed many of those boats and oilers have been shipwrecked and the crews of those ships of course are made up of foreigners and that does little for employment in Canada.
Just imagine that. Cl DA, an agency of the Canadian government, manages to find and send experts to Algeria to build a merchant marine in that country. I imagine it should not be too hard for the Algerians to outstrip us in this area. Flags of convenience have become a real plague. Some conventions and policies proposed or already applied in some countries have rid them of this plague. The UN has set up a maritime code providing that 80 per cent of the shipping between two countries should be done by vessels flying the flag of one or the other country, which leaves 20 per cent of the shipping to vessels flying other flags. But this convention has not been ratified by all trading nations. However, it indicates that there is a seemingly irreversible trend toward the protection of national interests in international shipping.
While many countries are combining money and efforts to build their merchant marine, our own government is moving at a snail's pace or not at all. We are really missing the boat, it is time to say. Even in the United States where 65 per cent of
January 29, 1979

shipping operations are carried out by vessels flying a flag of convenience, they have given thought to the establishment of an American merchant marine with a minimum quota for export-import shipping so that American sailors would have job opportunities rather than those from Elong Kong, Malaysia or other countries. With our potential, we only have to pluck up our courage and invest in setting up a merchant marine of our own.
In 1976, a project raised many hopes. It was the proposed construction of the M. V. Arctic. This ship was designed by a Montreal firm. Its construction was undertaken in the shipbuilding yard of Port Weller, Ontario, at a cost of $40 million. Three shipbuilding companies formed a consortium and, with federal government support, paved the way for the creation of a national merchant marine, and even if we had to call on technological expertise from abroad, even so this ship was nevertheless designed entirely in Canada and she was built in our own shipyards.
Mr. Speaker, that is really the first joint effort by the Canadian shipbuilding industry and the federal government. In an article published in La Presse on Friday, October 22, 1976, one could read this:
If the pilot project succeeds, the government intends to constitute a first nucleus of a national merchant marine with ten such vessels.
A few months earlier, on June 14, 1976, the vice-chairman of Canada Steamship Lines, Mr. Arthur Nightingale, stated at a seminar on transportation:
It is now economically possible to create a Canadian merchant marine regardless of any considerations of security and national sovereignty.
In spite of all his moderation and his carefulness, Mr. Darling had this to state in his report in 1974, and I quote:
It is obvious that the answer will not be the immediate creation and operation of a fleet under Canadian flag. But conditions are changing and it may be not only possible but also necessary that ships flying the Canadian flag operate within the international shipping community.
Mr. Darling had other comments to make which are still more to the point today. He noted that the companies that stood better in the international shipping community were those which were supported by their government, and I quote:
That means progressive penetration of nationalized or state-supported shipping companies will some day change considerably the competitive aspects in that industry.
On the question of costs, manpower, capital, expertise and shipyards we are just as advanced, Mr. Speaker, as our major trading partners. They are making increased efforts to develop their national fleets while we still only have an embryo which is far from being born, unfortunately. Following the release by the Minister of Transport of the report on our shipping policy in January, 1979, I wonder whether it is not more appropriate to talk of an abortion rather than a birth. Indeed, that report does not contain anything new and only maintains a status quo that has lasted long enough. The government refuses to recognize the need for new tax incentives.
The minister's release is a big disappointment. This is a time for action to use one of the prime minister's favorite slogans. This is a time for action, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the
Merchant Marine
formulation and the implementation of a real policy for the construction of a merchant marine in this country. The time has come and we have every reason to believe that in the future under bilateral agreements our partners will want to transport a percentage of our goods shipped abroad. If such is the case we will be in a very bad way. Without a fleet we will not be able to get reciprocity under such agreements. In 1974, we spent $2.7 billion to ship goods abroad. The greater part of that amount went to foreign shipping companies and their governments naturally which levy taxes. If one considers that shipping costs cannot be stable under the present economic conditions this will place our economy and our balance of payments in a shaky position.
In June, 1976, Canada Steamship Lines announced it was acquiring three merchant ships, and despite the good will of the company, it was regretfully announced that these ships would have to sail under a foreign flag. The vice-president of that company, whom I quoted earlier, explained the decision this way:
We waited in vain for 16 months for the federal government to take steps in line with the recommendations of the Darling report, and then we decided to go ahead.
Mr. Speaker, how can we explain then that Canadian ship owners cannot find here benefits comparable to those we are offering to foreign countries through the Export Development Corporation? In his report, Darling was referring to this and I quote:
Canadian companies flying foreign flags would not be prepared to change flag unless they were given the opportunity to make as much profit.
And further:
It is estimated that Canadian companies should be entitled to the credit of the Export Development Corporation at the same conditions as the ones offered to foreign companies buying Canadian vessels.
What Canadian companies want, Mr. Speaker, is just to get the same treatment as the one given to foreign competitors. At that point, a very specific recommendation from the Darling Report comes in, namely unification of responsibilities and the establishment of an authority with powers proportional to the various goals established to meet the needs of a merchant marine policy which should have as its first objective the establishment of a merchant marine in the country as it has been specified in my motion which is now under discussion. Our government keeps on thinking that the merchant marine is a sector as any other. It is a rare case, Mr. Speaker, in the club of industrialized nations. We have no specialized administration for all questions concerning international navigation. This lack of policy and this indecision are not to our credit. I have the impression that the government watches our merchant marine as one would watch somebody on his death bed. The problem of the merchant marine cannot be considered within the general scope of a transport policy. It is a specific problem which needs specific solutions.

Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) for having presented this motion which has been coming back before the

I have been saying, as reported in Le Peuple of Wednesday, February 12, 1975, some four years ago:
A solution must be found to this issue ...
I was giving an explanation in this article because it had reported one of the many speeches I made in the House concerning a Canadian merchant marine and it had recommended that the government should take a position.
I would first like to mention all the positive aspects of "A Shipping Policy for Canada" published by the Department of Transport under the authority of the Minister of Transport, Mr. Otto Lang. I think the hon. member for Rimouski should have seen some good things in this report, even though he thinks that it brings nothing new and that the government does not seem to be prepared to do anything. I think that all the debates we have had in the House lead to a recognition which is very important for the future of a Canadian merchant marine.
I would like to read from page 51 of the English version of this report which was published on January 24, 1979. The report says:
With respect to Arctic shipping, the government intends that, as a condition of approval to export unprocessed or partially processed resources, Canadian registered vessels must be used if they are available at reasonable cost. The government is also prepared to consider, on their merits and on an ad hoc basis, substantiated requests for assistance related to the use of ships both registered and built in Canada for use in the Arctic.
And this is a big step the government has just made. I will come back to this later on in the course of my review. It must be acknowledged, however, that the government wants to proceed with this issue. Indeed, it is stated on page 3 of the release issued by the government at the time the report was published:
The government finally concludes it would be appropriate to require for exportation ...
And I find also on the subject of
... the Arctic
But still, with respect to the ships we need for the Canadian merchant marine, it is stated under options 3- and 4, that if

there are changes in methods, if some countries want to go ahead at our expense either by forming groups against assistance or costs or by applying costs that could become prohibitive for the transportation of our export goods, the government would be ready to revise those policies at any time and put an end to that, and consideration must first be given to the national interests on policy matters concerning an ocean-going merchant fleet. This is all very good, and I will come back to this later. There is also a matter of savings.
Last week, I was allowed to ask a question of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). I asked him:
In view of the uncertainty which prevails regarding the future of Canada's shipbuilding industry and, in view of the many representations I have received from union spokesmen and shipyard officials, I would like to know if the government has made a decision concerning the 20 per cent subsidy to help shipbuilding in Canada and make us more competitive on the international market? Mr. Speaker, we have done a considerable amount of work on the drafting of a new shipbuilding policy. The Board of Economic Development Ministers and the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers want to make a comprehensive statement on the whole subject, possibly next Thursday.

We need this subsidy for the future of the Canadian shipyards. Let us look, Mr. Speaker, at recent newspaper head-

lines, and I would like to quote something that appeared quite recently, on January 23, in the newspaper La Presse:
Crisis-
-this appeared on January 23, 1979 in La Presse under the title:
HEAVY INDUSTRY:
Crisis in shipbuilding;
This article discussed in particular the future of the shipyards, and especially of the Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon, which is involved in shipbuilding for 70 per cent of its operations. The article said that if the government did not restore or permanently maintain the subsidy so that, as I said earlier, Canada can remain competitive internationally in the area of shipbuilding and conversion-I must recognize that while some people say that the government has not acted in this area, this subsidy was maintained by the hon. Jean-Luc Pepin and was extended by the hon. Jean Chretien when he was Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and was even amended because this 20 per cent subsidy previously applied only to shipbuilding and was extended to the conversion or modernization of Canadian ships and ships used for exports.
Mr. Speaker, I have here another newspaper. On a recent trip, I bought the November 25, 1978 issue of L'Express Information. On page 47 of the economic section, there was an article entitled:
The collapse of shipbuilding
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the future of our shipyards is a cause for concern if the government does not take some action. I cannot wait till Thursday and I shall be the first to applaud at anything that the government can do for an industry which is extremely important not only from an historical point of view, as the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) pointed out earlier, but also from an economic point of view and as regards the equipment needed on these ships. Indeed, we must not consider only the shipbuilding industry but also everything that it means for the secondary industry, all the supplies, all the subcontracts that the shipyards can let out when they are awarded important contracts, and most important, 80 per cent-I was even going to say 90 per cent, but I do not want to start an argument on figures-but our shipyards have been relying on government policies for their survival not only with respect to orders but also to incentives for shipbuilding, and it is truly essential for the future of this industry which is so important and deteriorating.
When I received a press release from the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association, I was quite pleased with the conclusions of this letter which was addressed to me and which expressed the association's concern. One could read in L'Express Information that before 1982, something which should certainly be a cause for great concern throughout the world, shipyards will be forced to close down. And such will be the case of our own shipyards too. We are not any wiser than the people in Europe where shipyards date back nearly a thousand years. Our own yards are hardly a few hundred years old. We also will be faced with this tragedy unless the govern-
Merchant Marine
ment acts and acts promptly. I was therefore very happy to see that the government had given some thought to the matter. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce told me last Thursday that the cabinet had looked into the problem as a result of the numerous representations I have been making for too long.
That is why I am pleased to see that the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) and other members are now concerned with the merchant marine. I am pleased to get their support, perhaps because we begin to have glimmers of hope, except for a few Conservative members and a few also on this side. We were a handful of members who believed that Canada could provide itself partially with a merchant marine, and I do hope that in the long run we shall have our own ocean merchant marine we can be proud of.
The Canadian Shipbuilding Association said the following in that letter they sent me: The long-term prospects in that area are excellent. The government will ensure that its fishing boats are replaced in the next five or ten years. We also expect to invest close to $1.5 billion in the building of six frigates to renew our merchant marine fleet for the marine department. We do know that this is a long-term policy, that there cannot be any immediate effects on shipbuilding. The government also intends to spend over $2 million on equipment, assistance and supplies of every description to develop Arctic resources. And I am convinced that a major part of those $2 million will be used, as the report signed by the Minister of Transport suggests, to transport our abundant natural resources in the Arctic.
So, Mr. Speaker, I too remain still concerned, at least until next Thursday, and if one wants to make an effort and still remain positive in all this matter, you will admit we made a big step. If the government can say that in an indefinite and unlimited way the subsidy will be maintained, as long as that subsidy of 20 per cent to assist the shipbuilding industry is amended, until we have really found the way in the short run to help the shipbuilding industry in Canada because we saw in the case of Marine Industries Limited what the government of Quebec has to do for that industry. And in that respect, Mr. Speaker, in a future debate I would like indeed to talk about the promises of a government in power. I do not want to enter the debate on the merchant fleet on that issue but I believe that those who will be my opponents and those who will have to fight the referendum in the riding of Levis and in the 16 ridings in and around Quebec City will have to answer very important questions with respect to the assistance to the shipbuilding industry, particularly when we know what they did; they awarded two contracts against a very firm recommendation to Marine Industries Limited when all recommendations said that contract should go to Davie Shipbuilding, for advantages not only as far as manpower is concerned but also for economic advantages.
Mr. Speaker, reporters, members in the Quebec City area are very saddened by what happened. But I am not provincially elected, I am federally elected, and I believe that more

Merchant Marine
than ever the people of Davie Shipbuilding at home, the people in the shipyards across Canada are beginning to recognize what we did and the debate we carried on with the support, that I carried on, I would say, with the support of a few members in this House today, is bearing fruit, and I am glad because we are going to reap them not only to the advantage of the hon. member for Levis. After 16 years, I believe I planted, as the popular saying goes, other seeds that bore fruit. That one took more time to grow but I think it is there and it is there to stay.
So, the government is doing something, contrary to what the hon. member for Rimouski has said, claiming that the status quo is being maintained, that things are at a standstill, that the government does not budge. 1 know the hon. member has been away from the House for a while due to illness. I am very happy to see that he is well again and I welcome him to the House. But to my mind, the first thing he should do is read in its entirety the report we published last week, because it points out critical aspects of the situation and, indeed, it makes positive suggestions. On that topic, I have always tried to be positive, Mr. Speaker, because when one is negative in a debate, one obtains nothing; nothing worth-while comes out of it.
Mr. Speaker, 1 feel the efforts I have made in this House have borne fruit. But they must be followed up. That report must not become just one amongst all the others. As some will notice, those who are listening to this debate, I avoided repeating my speech and shall not repeat it, because for me only one thing counts in this debate on our merchant marine: not the Darling report, not the mountains of other reports we have had, not all the studies and surveys we have made, but this report that can be criticized. Indeed, I should like to deal with it when 1 have more time, because this debate does not end today; we must come back to it, or at least to my motion, at which time I can continue-
