subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Like the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay), I am delighted that the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) has put a resolution of this sort on the order paper. I support it wholeheartedly. We have heard the hon. member for Levis on more than one occasion, as he has heard the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, the hon. member for Rimouski and the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), as well as many others on both sides of the House, speak in support of the proposition that Canada should have a merchant marine.
Perhaps I may be permitted to be a little critical, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member suggested that when we are critical we do not get what we want, that we should really go along with this government, accepting its little favours and be happy. Of course that is the paternal attitude of this government, that we should just take what it gives us.

I noted in the report published and distributed last week the minister said that for the movement of processed and partially processed goods for export from the Arctic every measure will be taken to ensure that they are carried on Canadian flag vessels. That is good and fine, and it is progress, but what progress! It is very slow. We have been addressing ourselves to this problem for years, it seems to me-at least six years to my knowledge, and the hon. member for Levis has said that for 15 years he has been working on the government and has only got this far. That is fine, but there is a puzzling paragraph in this particular report TP-1676 published last week in respect of a shipping policy for Canada, which I should like to quote.
At page 51 there are two quotations in respect of policy that I should like to put on the record. They both puzzle me. I do not know whether in the time allotted we will obtain any clarification. The first part states:
After full consideration of all of the factors involved, the government has concluded that, in the present circumstances achievement of these objectives does not warrant the provision of new tax or financial measures to support the development of a Canadian deep-sea merchant marine.
The objectives there refer to a Canadian flag fleet.
This is an admission that all the work done by the hon. member for Levis, except in respect of the Arctic, has gone unheeded by the government.
The second column on this same page 51 contains an extraordinary statement which I just do not understand at all. Perhaps someone will shed some light on it. It states:
The government intends to proceed with legislation to give it broad powers to obtain information and to act where Canadian shipping interests are threatened by the actions of a foreign government or carrier.
I suppose that is fair enough, but it goes on to
Legislation would include the power to permit the designation of "Canadian shipping lines", including companies located in Canada but not operating vessels under Canadian registry, to enable the government to respond to the requirements of a number of developing countries.
What sort of gobbledygook is this? We are going to have designated Canadian shipping lines. Under what flag are they to be operating, Panamanian or Peruvian? This government has to be out of its mind to come out with nonsense like that. Why does this government not provide some means for accomplishing the objective?
There are a number of means the government could adopt, three of which come to mind easily, to assist in the construction of Canadian vessels in Canadian yards for the creation of a Canadian merchant marine. The first means, of course, is through outright subsidy. I do not know what the Thursday declaration will be, but I hope, like the hon. member for Levis, the government will not cut back on this subsidy.
There is the second means, namely, tax incentives to those who are prepared to raise the capital for construction. That is the basis of the question I posed on January 25 in a supplement to a question raised by the hon. member for Levis.
The third method is one that is open to every other country in the world but not to Canadians, and that is the use of Canadian funds from the Export Development Corporation. Why is that the situation? We have built 51 ships within the
January 29, 1979

last four of five years for Greece, France, the United Kingdom, the Bahamas, Cuba, and Bermuda, and we have built them under the provisions of the Export Development Corporation. We have spent over $500 million in this regard, but we have not built one through that method, the Export Development Corporation, for a Canadian carrier. I wonder why is that. This is a misuse of Canadian funds. Why should Canadian corporations not have at their disposal the same facilities available to these other countries such as Cuba? Why should they not be able to get low interest credit and insurance coverage to guarantee loans? That is one of the methods used by the Export Development Corporation, the guaranteeing of loans.
When I was at home at Christmastime an enterprising man from the area who is interested in shipping came to me and said, "If I had a guarantee I could raise the money to obtain a small Canadian flag vessel, then perhaps another vessel, and then another." Unfortunately at this particular stage he is talking about buying vessels that are now afloat. That will not help our shipbuilding industry, I grant you, but once an individual gets started there is no end to it. It will grow, and before long we will be building our own ships. This was a very enterprising man and I listened to him carefully. He asked why the government would not guarantee a bank loan so he could buy a ship. He actually had Canadian cargoes for these ships.
Speaking of Canadian cargoes, I found some of the figures given in this particular study confusing. Am I to believe that imports into Canada, as described in the table at page 15 of this report, are brought into Canada on Canadian flag vessels to the extent of 47 per cent? I just cannot believe that. There are not that many Canadian flag vessels available.
On page 15 of the English version of this report under exports it is claimed that 21 per cent is carried on Canadian flag vessels. I have gone past Roberts Bank more times than I care to count and have seen Canadian coal piled ship high beyond the funnels for shipment to Japan, but I have not seen a single Canadian flag vessel carrying that coal. That coal is carried by Japanese vessels, which in turn bring back the steel processed by the use of that coal, some of that steel with four wheels and a steering wheel attached. This is our coal, and much of that is our steel from the British Columbia islands. It is all carried in foreign bottoms. We would certainly be able to carry the goods in Canadian bottoms if the matter of guaranteeing a bank loan for the construction of Canadian vessels were looked at carefully. I find that particular table very deceiving.
The table on page 44, also in the English version, mentions the route description and the export/import commodity. It brings us right back to the coal I mentioned which was being carried from Roberts Bank to Japan. Coal is carried to Japan and the ships come back empty. We import a great deal from Japan. Why do we not carry the coal in Canadian bottoms and bring back the cars and the televisions, if that is what we are
Merchant Marine
importing from Japan? That table on page 44 is a disgrace, and should not be included in a study of this sort.
The hon. member may be content with what this government has done to ensure as much as possible and at reasonable cost, the carriage of Arctic resources. His minister has sold him a bag of garbage. It is not a guarantee that all our imports and exports into the Arctic will be carried on Canadian vessels. That report is a great deception and letdown after the Darling report, which has been urging the creation of a merchant marine. There are other reports, such as the Audette report, and the situation goes back longer than either of us can probably remember.
I understand that we have guarantees from some of the labour unions for "X" number of years that there be a no-strike clause in' the contract, because that is one of the things which destroyed our merchant marine after the war.
I know there are other members who will want to speak on this subject. Once again I would like to thank the hon. member for Rimouski for bringing this matter forward. This government does not have the time to create a policy on this matter, but there is one being developed. I can assure hon. members of that, but they will have to wait for the results of the election to see it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the previous speakers to thank the member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) who was the mover of the motion today. I think it is an excellent opportunity to do so, since Canadian policy on maritime transport was made public last week. I also take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to welcome him back after his illness and assure him we are ready to cross swords in a friendly way as usual.
As for his comments, Mr. Speaker, as my colleague for Levis (Mr. Guay) has pointed out, I think he should have paid more attention to the report recommendations with respect to a Canadian policy on maritime transport, because it is far from advocating the status quo and I believe, for example, that restricting the shipping of resources from or to Northern Canada to Canadian ships is a major step in the right direction.
The hon. member for Levis, as usual when the subject especially concerns him, made an impassioned speech, and I would like to say on behalf of all my colleagues, that he has shown great perseverance in his long and useful career as a member of parliament in bringing up a subject which concerns of course the interests of his constituency, but which also is of great importance for the economic future and direction of the whole country.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) talked garbage in his speech. I shall mention only the venom which we are used to seeing him pour forth periodically in this House. We had rather a good example of this last

January 29, 1979
Merchant Marine
Friday in his speech about the bill on referendum, and this only added to the outpouring of venom contained in his few comments today.
Before speaking specifically about the direction of our policy concerning the merchant fleet, I would like to rectify a figure mentioned by my colleague from Rimouski, who said that there were only three oceanic ships sailing under the Canadian flag. I would like to tell him the good news and announce that there has been a fourth ship sailing under the Canadian flag since early January, and I would like to quote in regard to an article in the newspaper Le Devoir of January 5 and written by Mr. Guy Deshaies, which says the following:
An important even though modest step in the development of a Canadian merchant fleet will be made this weekend when the ship Maurice Desgagnes, sailing under the Canadian flag, leaves the port of Chicoutimi loaded with wood pulp and explosives for the Netherlands and Germany.
The ship will come back from its first international trip with a full load of German import products.
Mr. Speaker, this is a new company called Desgagnes Maritime Limitee and I am very happy to mention this fact because this company is established in my constituency and has been active in shipbuilding since the beginning of this century. Moreover, the chairman of the Desgagnes group, Mr. Yvan Desgagnes, has always been an active supporter of the merchant fleet. We must depend on the entrepreneurship of Canadian entrepreneurs, on the quality of our labour as mentioned by the hon. member for Rimouski, as we realize that even a private company in a less privileged area of Canada succeeded in carrying the Canadian ensign on international seas and, I am very proud of it as it is a company from my riding.
Mr. Speaker, 1 do not have the time to undertake an exhaustive analysis of the report published last week as I have only three minutes left, but I wish to say very briefly that in view of the adverse situation of the shipping industry, considering that there are too many vessels used for international transportation and that many companies do not succeed in obtaining contracts anymore and that, in the last three years, international shipping companies have seen their profits decrease, in view of the adverse situation of the shipping industry and the fact that it would be difficult to prove that a Canadian merchant fleet would be the ideal answer to our problems, to our balance of payments or our present commercial problems, the new financial or fiscal measures to encourage oceanic transportation by ships flying the Canadian Hag are not justified economically. Investments in oceanic transportation do not represent an optimum use of our national resources. This is an important factor as the government tries to encourage economic development through a minimum of interference.

Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock, when the House adjourned for supper, I was saying that in the Conservative policy-if it is really a policy-relating to the bill, to what the government is saying on the constitutional issue, on the national unity issue, the objective is not to put forward a viable alternative, to tell Canadians exactly what they want to do, but simply to attack what the government proposes, pretending as the Leader of the Opposition himself stated this afternoon, that the Liberal party is only trying to get some electoral capital. Yet, Mr. Speaker, they are playing politics with national unity, not the Liberal party, and I for one will not try to find an excuse because my leader has a viable position concerning the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, here I will be critical of my own colleagues and many Liberals across the country who should stop apologizing because our leader, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is an efficient critic-as he has always been-of political nationalism in Quebec. Time has come to stop apologizing for that. 1 do not feel ashamed because the leader of the Liberal party can say across Canada: here is the policy of the Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative party should realize that by limiting themselves to criticizing our position on this issue without even putting forward a viable alternative, they show their weakness, their inability to arrive at positions. Mr. Speaker, there are ramifications to constant frustration of constitutional reform and constant downgrading of its importance. Before the five o'clock recess, I was suggesting I find it very hard to control my temper when I hear people state in or outside the House that the issue of national unity, the issue of the constitution is not that important and there are other matters more important to discuss.
Mr. Speaker, I also dealt with perceptions of injustice in Canadian history. There are not only, however, perceptions of past injustice, there are real injustices perpetrated now today on language matters, on racial matters in Canada. If anybody is amazed or questions this, let them come to my province where I could point to examples. I would quite simply suggest that perhaps the Progressive Conservatives are naive-because I am not in any way intimating they are being devious-they probably are naive if they think they can maintain a united and strong Canada while frustrating endlessly the constitutional reform process.
With regard to the statements made by the Leader of the Opposition over the past few months about sovereignty-association, there is an article in La Presse of October 28, 1978, in which he is reported by Mr. Louis Falardeau as having said something he has never denied, in spite of everything he is trying to say now:
Referenda
I shall have a mandate to negotiate with the provinces, and if a province has a specific mandate, I shall have to negotiate and deal with it.
Then many people have taken to task the new and unfortunate member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), a former mayor of the city of Toronto, who has not yet adjusted to federal politics. I do not blame him for his blunder, because he was doing exactly like his leader. I suggest that his leader did not mean any harm when he said that, because he did not realize what he was saying. I merely say that he is irresponsible and naive and proves his inadequacy as a national leader. That is what I am saying of the Leader of the Opposition.
Mr. Speaker, I have always been against any action leading to political isolation. I have always objected to those who wanted to isolate people because of their language or their culture. However, I can understand as a Francophone how easy it was for political parties such as the separatist party in Quebec to inject nationalism in politics. It is quite easy to understand when one looks for five minutes at Canadian history. If anyone can deny that there never have been and there still do not exist in this country attitudes that are not as favourable to the French fact as they could have been, it is because he is not being honest. Surely one can hide this fact and pretend it does not exist. But it does exist, Mr. Speaker. That is why I think national parties such as the Progressive Conservative party should make its position clearly known on this particular issue.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to constitutional reform, it is getting late for Quebeckers as well as for Francophones outside Quebec, because they feel that some things ought to be changed in our country. And I explained earlier that the Progressive Conservative party always says when this matter is discussed: Look who has been in power for 10, 12 or 15 years, you have. And they seem to blame us for it. I told them that it was impossible to mean-

speechtext:
Some Conservative members are helping me make my point. What they do not realize is that one cannot redress the political institutions of this country nor can one redress the political order of this country without creating tension. If hon. members think they can do that, they are fooling themselves. One cannot do that unless tensions are created.

The fact that tensions have been created in this country for the last ten or 12 years does not worry me at all. There were tensions in my own provinces also, and that does not worry me too much either. There were some reactions against the promotion of Acadians. Looking at New Brunswick politics, it is obvious that there were some reactions like those. We should not worry about that. Such things are normal. If we are
2672

January 29, 1979
Referenda
seeking, a healthy society, we should not hesitate to tell each other truth. What happened in Canada for the last ten years is that we have begun to tell each other the truth. When truth is told, it is normal that some people try to use the truth to break the country. It is true that we have seen tensions, and it is true that we will know some more. Why? Because Canadians have started to face the truth and recognize it. These are the steps that we have to go through if we want to be able to take real decisions on those matters.
Unfortunately, the Progressive Conservative party is making an electoral issue out of that bill, out of the constitutional question. They are the ones who make an electoral issue of that question. The recent remarks of the Leader of the Opposition and of the hon. member for Rosedale, although they both tried to clarify them, have shown that they are unable to understand the situation in Quebec and in Canada, that they are unable to really lead this country as a responsible party.

Earlier in my speech I mentioned that I had suggested a couple of days after the November 15, 1976, election that the federal government had a duty to make sure that the people of Quebec could respond to their federal government as well as to their provincial government. Why? Because now that the PQ have the means of communication in Quebec and the means of development, the government can create a context into which it could convince Quebeckers that the federal system is against their interests. That is exactly what I thought at the time and that is exactly what has happened. If hon. members want an example of what I meant at the time-and it is still an issue today-they could take a look at the issue of transmission of electricity from Newfoundland to Canadian markets and U.S. markets. We know that there was a deal made for Churchill Falls, and while I do not necessarily agree totally with the position of Quebec, I can agree that on that one, a deal is a deal and a contract is a contract. It is difficult to deny that.
But what about the development of the Lower Churchill- Gull Island?
That power will have to be transmitted through Quebec on Quebec land. Do hon. members not realize that it is possible in that kind of a context to make that an issue in Quebec and convince Quebeckers that it is against their direct interests to be part of a federal system? They can, and if hon. members do not know that, they do not know what is happening in Quebec. That is exactly the kind of issue around which the PQ could create a referendum campaign. In this instance, Quebeckers, if they want to be good Canadians will probably give Newfoundland a break and give Newfoundland what it is due so it can sell its resources in Canada and in the United States. That is an issue around which the Quebec government can very skillfully convince Quebeckers that a federal system is against their direct interest. It may not be against their indirect interests as citizens of Canada but it can be against their interests strictly as Quebeckers. That is why the federal government has a duty and a responsibility to make sure that on the question of the future of Quebec the federal government

must ask that question of Quebeckers as much as their provincial government will.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude on that point. Some people say that it is up to the Quebec people to decide their own fate. I heard a member make that comment this afternoon, I do not argue against that, naturally, because it will be mostly up to Quebeckers to decide.
But the fact is, Mr. Speaker, that I am a Francophone, and like other Canadians also, I have a right to speak to Quebeckers before they make up their minds because a part of Quebec belongs to me, my own history is rooted in Quebec and I have always felt that the fact that Quebec was the stronghold of the Francophone community in North America, in Canada, has inspired me personally and politically.
Mr. Speaker, French speakers outside Quebec have something to say on this matter; I am not suggesting that we tell Quebeckers that they are not able to make their own decision, but rather that I have the right to speak to them before they give their final word. In that sense, the bill that we are debating today is important because of the authority it would give the federal government, and parliament-in spite of what the Leader of the Opposition was saying this afternoon, to mislead the people-to decide when and how a referendum would be held, first on the future of Quebec, if necessary, but also on constitutional reform. I categorically oppose the Leader of the Opposition's attitude and position when he says that if two or three provinces want to boycott the progress of constitutional reform in Canada parliament should accept that. Parliament has something to say in this regard, and this is an important bill, Mr. Speaker, which concerns not only a referendum on the future of Quebec but also possible referenda on consitutional reform. We must not let those who want to destroy Canada impede the reform of Canadian political institutions, because those people want to use the diversity of Canada, which should be our strength, to destroy the country. That is what they want to do.
Mr. Speaker, we have the responsibility as a federal government, as a federal parliament, because in this parliament there are people from all over the country who spend days, weekends, weeks or election campaigns to go and persuade Canadians in all parts of the country to elect them to sit in this parliament, and I do not accept at all the idea that only the provincial governments can speak on behalf of the Canadian people.
Each hon. member is elected here to speak on behalf of Canadians, and if at a certain time partisan provincial politicians are only thinking about the future of their own province and if, on the other hand, we see, as it is the case in Quebec today, a government which wants to isolate Quebeckers around their language and their culture, which is bad for the future of Canada, it is our responsibility to have a mechanism enabling us to go and ask the people of Quebec what they
January 29, 1979

want, to ensure that the context in which that question is asked will favour those who want to fight for the unity of Canada, not only in a context which will favour those who want to dismantle the country. That is the danger. And the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) talks about respecting Canada's diversity. He says the government's attitude on the constitutional reform, on the subject matter of this bill, is dangerous because it does not respect Canada's diversity. I asked him this afternoon: Diversity at what price? Diversity until when? Diversity to what extent?
There is a danger of too strong a decentralization and of too strong a concern over this diversity, when one relies only on provincial governments to express this diversity, it is dangerous, it is naive, it is irresponsible. Each and every member of parliament represents the diversity of Canadians, wherever he may sit in the House. Where are these people elected? Where do they exercize their political ability? In any part of the country. We express here the diversity of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, for Quebec's future as well as for constitutional reform, we need a tool which will enable us to go to Canadians and ask them: What do you want? Do you want what your provincial government proposes? If, as I was saying a moment ago, a provincial government wants to hinder the constitutional reform, for their own reasons, should we, as the federal parliament, accept this? I say no, Mr. Speaker, and I would like those who pretend to be speaking in favour of a strong and united country to say the same.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate on Bill C-9, an act respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada. The most important words in that title are "relating to the Constitution of Canada." The title of the bill must be read in conjunction with what is being put forward, as stated so eloquently by our national leader this afternoon.
I have just finished listening to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). I noticed that in most of his speech he was very critical. His aim in presenting his argument on unity and on this bill was to hurl reproaches and recriminations at the Conservative party rather than getting down to what is in the bill and under study this evening. It will not be my purpose in speaking tonight to hurl reproaches and recriminations at the Liberals, only to allude to one.
Since 1963 under Pearson that party was the government. Since 1968 under Trudeau they have been in the government. Prior to that time the question of unity was not in the form of confrontation and disunity that we have today. Regardless of what they say, they must bear some responsibility for the status of this issue in Canada at the present time.
At the outset I would like to read the most important part of the bill, and this was dealt with by our leader this afternoon
Referenda
when dealing with the title of the bill, the Constitution of Canada and how far it goes. I quote from clause 2:
"Constitution of Canada" includes, without limiting the meaning of that expression,
(a) the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of Canada,-
Our leader mentioned the various customs and precedents of parliament. The traditions and customs that crystallize the democratic process we have in this country should be one of the terms and matters placed before the people of Canada.
The word "enactments" in the bill means any bill that has been enacted by this parliament, whether it be the Bill of Rights or any other bill.
The point that bears emphasis, and I draw the attention of the chamber to this, is the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada. The political institutions are the institutions of this parliament. The judicial institutions are all the other parts of our democratic system. That means this bill is really a general referendum bill. That is the complaint our party is placing on record in this debate. We are not against a referendum in any shape or form if the matter placed before the Canadian people is a special act or a special matter rather than on general matters. Therein lies the difference in the position between our leader and our party and the arguments from the other side.
One of the first things we must do is look at the word constitution as defined in the bill. What are we really talking about? I would like to put a couple of definitions on record before getting to the meat of what I intend to say about this bill. What does the word constitution mean? I would like to read from a book by J. D. Whyte and W. R. Lederman, "Canadian Constitutional Law". I quote:
The word constitution... means the document in which are set out the rules governing the composition, powers and methods of operation of the main institutions of government, and the general principles applicable to their relations to the citizens.
That is a very good, succinct, and brief definition of what the word constitution means. There are other definitions. There is the definition of Salmond in "Jurisprudence", and 1 quote:
Constitutional law is, as its name implies, the body of those legal rules which determine the constitution of the state.
That means the physical make-up of this country, which is exactly what our constitution is all about.
There is another definition by Dicey, which I will put on record at the same time:
Constitutional law ... appears to include all rules which directly or indirectly affect the distribution or the exercise of the sovereign power in the state.
I wish to deal with three aspects. First, I will deal with the make-up of our country. I will then give some historical background. I heard some this afternoon from the hon. member for Gloucester and from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General (Mr. Collenette). What really is the make-up of this country? As I have said on many occasions in this chamber, we are not made up of provinces totally,

Referenda
although there are ten provinces in our present system. We are made up of regions.
We are all part of all that we are. Each is needed by the other, and nothing is good alone. The prairie provinces have certain ideas about this country. The Pacific province of British Columbia has certain ideas. Ontario has certain fundamental ideas about it. I have listened to many speeches in this House, not only in this debate but in others. Quebec certainly has some definite ideas about the make-up of Canada, and so it should. The Atlantic provinces naturally have certain ideas.
I listened to the reproaches and recriminations hurled across the aisle this afternoon. I will not engage in that. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) made a very learned, reasonable and, I might say, low key speech on this issue. We live in a healthy climate. Canadians from region to region present their arguments and positions. We are all part of the environment.
I listened today to the hon. member for York East. He talked about being born in the United Kingdom. Well, many of us have roots there. But there is a difference he does not seem to appreciate and 1 should like to put it on record. It is plain, it is easy. Most of us understand it, but sometimes one has to argue from a known premise when one is developing an idea. It is that we are operating under a federal system. How did that system come about? We did not unite as a country, that is, the provinces of Canada, Upper and Lower Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, just because we all loved one another-though no doubt, we respected one another's rights. We came about as a nation because of the growth of North America. At that time there was springing up to the south a very strong nation, one of the strongest in the western world, the United States-and thank goodness it is strong. So we were able to compromise.
As I read history, John A. Macdonald felt at the beginning that we should establish a legislative union. What is a legislative union? A legislative union is one where all powers are centralized in one government and then delegated to the various provinces and municipalities. A federal union is a central government with delegated authority under the distribution of powers, other powers being delegated to the provinces so that each area will have its say. Therein lies the difference between legislative and federal union. And when Macdonald and Cartier, an English-speaking Canadian on one hand and a French-speaking Canadian on the other, recognized that the four areas I have mentioned should come together as a nation, they came together under a compromise arrangement because each was able to make concessions; we were able to bring this country together by uniting the four provinces I have mentioned, and later the other regions came in, one after another.
If we were able to accomplish this without a referendum, do we need the kind of referendum which the government is proposing? I am not against a referendum, but do we need the kind of general referendum which would allow us as a parlia-

ment to make a decision? I want to ask this further question: do we, as a parliament, really make the decision? I say it is the cabinet which draws up the questions. Ministers draft the questions and bring them before parliament, knowing full well at this time that they command a majority and that they may have some help from the New Democratic Party which, as I understand it, is split this afternoon. So it is the government which will set the questions, and that is what I call a general referendum and that is what I am complaining about in connection with the bill before us.
We want the people to have their say. We believe in conferences, we believe in consultation. The government has held many conferences with the provinces in connection with confederation. Those who took part were not able to agree, but they agreed on some things, and arrangements are presently in hand for the holding of a further conference in February. Now we are to have a general referendum. Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada certainly want to have their say, if they are asked specific questions and if those questions could be brought before parliament by way of a special act in which they would be set up. Some people in this country believe there should be a referendum on the issue of capital punishment-yes or no. 1 see an hon. member over there shake his head. Maybe he would not want that kind of referendum to be held.
I say that if there is to be a special referendum asking, say, a question concerning the distribution of powers as between the federal and provincial governments, let the question be placed specifically before parliament by way of a special act. This was done at the time of prohibition, and the same was done on the conscription issue. Canadians would then know where they stood. But to give the government the power to hold a general referendum whereby they themselves draft the questions is unacceptable. I am reminded of the question, "Have you stopped beating your wife?" If you say yes, you are wrong. If you say no, you are wrong. And then members opposite say, "Of course, parliament is going to decide."
Well, Mr. Speaker, parliament is going to decide, because we are allowed 40 hours of debate in parliament, and they were not even content with putting the guillotine rule of 40 hours into force. They even told the Senate they had to shape up in 40 hours, too. And then you know what it means, Mr. Speaker. They say parliament decides. Ladies and gentlemen, it is all decided nicely in the back rooms, to use an expression which one hon. member used this afternoon-somebody accused the Conservatives of back room tactics; well, if they did use some back room tactics they had some great teachers over there. So what is going to happen? The government is going to draft the questions. It is going to make a political ploy, and that is not what we are prepared to accept in this bill at this stage. That is why we intend to vote against it.
To get back to the question of a federal union, the issue can again be put in simple terms. All those matters that are common to Canadians in the ten provinces from coast to coast are matters for the central government, and all those that are local are matters for the provincial governments. Of course there is always some overlapping. It would take me a couple of
January 29, 1979

hours in which to read even a summary of the cases on the Constitution of Canada which have been decided in the last 30 years. They have gone to the Supreme Court of Canada, and some of the eariier ones have been referred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. When I see before me wording such as I have read to the Elouse with reference to the Constitution of Canada-and meaning the constitution as defined by this bill, not by the definition 1 have read in Dicey or Jennings-I, as a Canadian, become very concerned and I think every Canadian who listens to the speech I am making now will be most concerned, wherever he or she may live.
As I have mentioned, only two referenda have been held. There was one on prohibition in 1928, and Quebec voted against the idea. 1 might say that had I taken part I would have voted against it too. I say this because prohibition did more to undermine the morals of this country than anything else has done.

next election? Every single Conservative knows that. I said that I wanted to finish on the subject matter of the Conservative party position on the Pepin-Robarts commission. I want to go to the next election, and I want something very clear from the Conservative party. I want to hear the Conservatives say that.
What I am saying, and as far as I know what every member of this government is saying, is that we think the purpose of a nation state is to serve the citizens. The best thing any nation state can do for any citizen is to make sure it is the servant of the citizen and not the master. The only way that can be ensured is by having civil rights enshrined in a constitution. Mr. Speaker, 112 years ago, the Fathers of our Canadian Confederation met to unite those two Canadas and lay the foundation of confederation. One thing is sure: they were members of various political parties, and came from different areas of the country.

It goes without saying that the Fathers of Confederation 112 years ago, coming as they did from different political parties and different regions of the country, were obviously proud and were loyal to the various regions from which they came. In a spirit of bipartisan statesmanship and broad vision, however, they gave birth to this country that we today call Canada. I am sure that the one message the Fathers of Confederation would give to us in this House today would be that we should reincarnate that spirit, that bipartisan statesmanship and broad vision-we should bury the hatchet to a certain extent and get on with building a new Canada. We must bury the hatchet and speak together about one Canada.
We are not going to agree on all points, of course. I am as guilty of it as the next person, but quite often I do not like the atmosphere there is in this House. I think each and every one of us in this House is a good Canadian. No one is better than the other. No one indispensable man is going to save this union. No one party is indispensable. If, in a spirit of partisanship, we continue yelling across the floor to each other on this issue, and possibly having a referendum on it, only one person is going to be laughing on his way to the referendum, and that is Rene Levesque.
Maybe we have the fathers and mothers of the new confederation sitting in this House today, Mr. Speaker. 1 think we do. I have friends on both sides of this House who are capable of exhibiting the kind of statesmanship and determination that is going to set this country on new roads. The Fathers of Confederation would be the first to tell us-
[ Translation]
-to work together here in the House of Commons. In the broader sense of the word, a constitution is, let us say, a political document, in the best sense of the word. But it seems to me, in view of the challenge we now face as Canadian politicians, that we must work together, in the real sense of the word, towards a renewed federalism.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, let me say that it will be very difficult for me to discuss openly what will follow here in the House of Commons, but I start my speech with a deep sense of responsibility as the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi whose population is about 75 per cent Francophone and 25 per cent Anglophone, a riding where the two linguistic groups of our country live together, as in Sherbrooke, in a true spirit of national unity.

The eastern townships, Bonaventure and other parts of the province, are not necessarily typical as opposed to those areas that are unilingual, be they unilingual French-speaking or English-speaking, but through our historical evolution, be it social, political, economic or constitutional, the people in my part of the world, as the hon. member opposite just said, like in many parts of Quebec, have learned to live together in a true, constructive, and positive spirit of national unity.
National unity in debates like this is quite difficult for me to talk about. It is something that for years people in my part of the country have felt deeply about and deeply believed in. It has dominated our political activities.

And I am proud, as is the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) to represent here, in this House of Commons, such a spirit of national unity. But that spirit demands, Mr. Speaker, the word is slightly more English, I know, that spirit demands leadership.

What we find in the eastern townships and in my riding is that when Canadians of the two different language groups get to know each other-it is not always easy because of the make-up of our country-it is living proof of what can be done in a true and constructive spirit of Canadians working together in national unity.
Let us have a good open debate about this. I am no better a Canadian than any member opposite, but if I differ in some details-and after all they are only details-my desire to preserve this union we call Canada is no less than theirs. We are not getting the kind of leadership we need if all we can do here today is draft a referendum, or draft legislation for a referendum, or from a federal viewpoint address ourselves to the proposition of a provincial referendum being held and asking Canadians a question which they do not want to be asked. Hon. members may feel 1 am presumptuous in saying that. I say this for the second time: Why ask the people of Canada a question, the answer to which we already know? Why ask the people a question they do not want us to ask them?

Mr. Speaker, when I took my oath of office here in Ottawa, as an elected member of the House of Commons I promised to

preserve national unity directly and indirectly. Together with hon. members from both sides of the House, I promised also to defend and define-or more appropriately under the present circumstances-redefine the federal entity.

When I was sworn in as a member of Parliament in Ottawa at the beginning of this parliament, I understood directly and indirectly that implicit in being sworn into this House was my promise to the Canadian people at large, and to my constituents in particular, that I was to defend and define-and as the circumstances are here right now, redefine-the federal cause. The people of my constituency never asked me to ask them the most stupid possible question: "Do you Heward, or do the people up in Ottawa want this union to continue?" Instead of passing this kind of legislation and instead of heading into the kind of trouble which I do not want to contemplate, especially in my particular part of the world- and I will choose my language later-I plead with hon. members opposite to forget this insanity, reach out across the floor of this House and include us in the debate on constitutional renewal. God only knows that much sooner than later and no matter who is in power after the next election, the whole idea of a plebiscite or a referendum could easily become an academic hypothesis. We are called on to lead.
What is the government asking for in this legislation? Is it asking for vague powers to hold a referendum? When I am asked to address myself to a debate, I want to know the ground rules. I want to know with some modicum of precision what I am asked to do. Is this bill about the desire of the government to change unilaterally our constitutional framework? I do not know. I suspect it is not. Most hon. members are honest and realistic enough to say what this bill is about. It is a specific reaction to what is going on in my province. I ask again what every member from this side of the House has asked since this debate was initiated, if that is the case, why not-

I urge the right hon. Prime Minister to forget this bill as soon as possible.

The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) referred to past plebiscites. This is one of the saddest days in my life as a parliamentarian. It really is. I say this with no partisan gratification; this is a sad day for me. I make no apology for my emotion. But in a sense I may be able to influence directly and indirectly those who come to Ottawa. I know one thing, if this atmosphere persists in the House over various policies, as I noted a moment ago, there is only one man who stands to gain and that is Rene Levesque, the present premier of Quebec. [English]
There is one question that is asked of me by members opposite, admittedly by the public, and very often by the press. Where does your party stand on these questions of national unity, constitutional development, and federal-provincial relations? Maybe in some small detail we differ with members opposite. When I think about, as we say in French-
[ Translation]
-the main tenets of our policy-

-we are all together as good Canadians. In committee we can discuss our detailed differences on these issues. However, if we are looking for semantic slips or whatever in order to wage an election on this issue, forget Canada my friends. The Fathers of Confederation never did it. Why should we? The crisis, emergency and challenge facing us are no less than the challenge that faced them. I am often accused of being an alarmist. However, even in my part of the world we have slowly come to the realization that time is not on our side.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was first elected in 1965, I had great admiration for him. I still have a great deal of admiration for him. He is a personal friend. I met him many times in the cafeteria upstairs in this building, knowing that he had the ear of the then prime minister. I told him that I had been in this House for seven years and that I was appalled at the duplication, buck passing and waste as between the federal authorities and the provinces.
Apart from the specific things going on in my province at the time, a succession of Quebec governments were saying this is the last chance for Canada, with varying degrees of nationalistic slogans. I pleaded with the then parliamentary secretary to the prime minister to lend his considerable weight to the urgent demands of the time for immediate constitutional reform. Frankly, he disagreed with me. He said, "Heward, we have a constitution now which provides enough flexibility for what I want to do, and by confrontation with the provinces I would create an atmosphere and mix that would end up in no progress."

We have had 14 years of that kind of confrontation. I am not saying this in a partisan sense, but frankly, Mr. Speaker, every member of this House must realize it has not worked. Nobody can objectively say that it is working very well. The chickens are home to roost and the time has surely come for us to consider that constitutional renewal that we considered 14 years ago. Again I ask, what is the government asking us to pass?

With many members in the past, I have voted against the constitutional implications of orders in council, a bill not having the regulations presented so that we would know the substance of it, or omnibus legislation with many subjects under one heading. The present bill is the final insult. Why not take us into your confidence? What do you want I ask? [Translation]
What do you want? The legislation under study in the House is so vague that I cannot see its substance.

It is very difficult to ask responsible members of parliament on either side of the House to pass legislation that is so vague that the substance will only begin to make sense when civil servants, under the instructions of the government of the day, write in regulations. I have already mentioned the Prohibition Plebiscites Act of 1898.

Then, as the hon. lady from Kingston and the Islands said in her magnificent speech, came the 1942 conscription issue and, by amendment, the Dominion Plebiscite Act of 1942 actually went as far as to write in the question though leaving the time of the calling of the plebiscite to the government of the day. The question and the intent of the act were clear. What it did in substance to our country is another thing.

After the plebiscite, the prime minister at that time said: conscription if necessary but not necessarily conscription. Today with such a legislation we may be facing another issue, Mr. Speaker: separation if necessary, but not necessarily separation.

This, Mr. Speaker, is the most disruptive, ambiguous and damaging piece of legislation in this whole area that the government could possibly have brought up. In my appeal for a bipartisan approach to constitutional renewal-I do not think it is too late-let me say this: hon. members opposite

should not dignify the validity of referenda, be they federal or provincial, by passing one here in Ottawa. I have no idea what the provincial referendum is going to be in the province of Quebec. I have no idea.

I am sorry, but my time is limited. Without drawing a long bow I will attempt to show how ridiculous is what we are attempting to do. In this electronic age it is very arguable that we do not need a House of Commons. I am not going to get into a philosophical debate, as to whether part of the country has a right to secede or the efficacy or lack of efficacy of referenda in a so-called British parliamentary system. But it is a fact of life that in an electronic age, leaving aside Mr. Orwell's 1984, it is highly conceivable that within two hours we could ascertain public opinion on any issue facing the country as a result of people voting from their living rooms. If members want to get into that type of direct democracy, even political parties today could pay for more sophisticated polls than the Gallup polls. You know, Mr. Speaker, and I know it. Electronic polls could be held on any issue.
The most serious plea I have ever made in my public life is to ask members opposite to forget this insanity. It is absolute insanity. I have talked to Canadians of both linguistic groups across my province, and I can only say that by dignifying the validity of referenda along the lines of the bill before us the government will be giving Mr. Levesque a weapon that he never expected to have. He has said he will continue to hold them provincially until he wins. So let us get together and defend and define the federal cause. We shall be doing that not by asking the people questions they do not wish to be asked but by working together for that degree of constitutional renewal Canadians are seeking.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-"THE ROAD AHEAD" CIRCULATED BY FORMER MINISTER OF FINANCE
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-"THE ROAD AHEAD" CIRCULATED BY FORMER MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the adjournment debate in which I take part tonight arises from an exchange in this House between the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and I on December 21 last. At that time I referred the Minister of Finance to the latest of the letters which had been sent out by his predecessor twice removed, Mr. Turner, with respect to the haphazard, inadequate, and inept handling of the economy on the part of this government, and I was very much surprised to find that rather than dealing with the substance of Mr. Turner's comments concerning the Canadian economy and the inadequacies of the government, the Minister of Finance chose to use quips to try, somehow or other, to conceal the true impact of what Mr. Turner had been alleging.

Hon. members will recall that the Minister of Finance said that the letter to which I was referring, as he said was the case with other Turner letters, amounted only to a gossip column which one could get from any newstand in Toronto for 15 cents. I pointed out to the Minister of Finance at that time that the price was not 15 cents but that it was actually $15,000 to each of the corporate elite to whom Mr. Turner had been sending this information, and that in truth Mr. Turner had been making substantial revenues from circulating his comments concerning the government to this group of corporate brass of executives at $15,000 each. It was estimated that there may have been 12 to perhaps as many as 20 recipients.
I put a further question to the Minister of Finance, and again he made an offhand comment concerning the letters. The reason I asked that this be put down for adjournment debate is that I feel it is not so much a matter of embarrassment to the government to have a former minister of finance, who in many quarters is still respected, making comments concerning the present economic stance of this government- that perhaps is secondary-but to me the important thing is that these comments are being made not only by Mr. Turner and not only by economists from coast to coast but also in questions and speeches in this House continually, yet the government is evading the answers.
The government is not levelling with the Canadian public. Why, for example, is our dollar now in the 83 cent range, the lowest level it has been at on an average annual basis for over 120 years? Why, over the last few years, has our economic performance been worse than that of any of the major industrial nations of the world? The November 16 budget of the Minister of Finance forecast a $25 billion deficit for this year and the coming year. That happens to be a deficit on non-capital expenditures amounting to 25 per cent of the total expenditures of the government over the next two years.
Without any hesitation, on November 17 and continually thereafter, we in this party have said that that is an intolerable deficit, and that the government must answer to the Canadian public as to why it has been totally inadequate in curbing that deficit. That is the position of my party.
If the Minister of Finance does not have the courage to come into the House tonight and answer the question as to why the government has put us into this type of deficit position, at least his parliamentary secretary can somehow or other bring the word. Surely it is not enough, day in and day out, to question the Minister of Finance concerning not only the falling dollar and the $25 billion non-capital deficit which he forecast for the nation this year and next, but also concerning rising inflation, rising unemployment and the current account deficit.
In a document entitled "The Road Ahead", the former minister of finance, Mr. John Turner, indicated the following at page 3:
January 29, 1979

Finally, there is apparently a mood for a pro-business budget-The crux is the size of the federal deficit. The government does not wish it to exceed the present public projection-
As far as the public is concerned, the crux is the intolerable deficit which the government has asked Canadians to bear. I will be interested in hearing the remarks of the parliamentary secretary tonight. How can he justify the 25 per cent of the total expenditure deficit? As I have said, it is revealed in the November 16 budget.
In a nutshell, it is time for the government to be candid with the Canadian public. If it has mismanaged the public purse, it is time to admit it, ask for forgiveness, and have an election to clear the air. As Mr. Turner has said, it is intolerable to have the present inadequate handling of our economy without an election, although an election has been anticipated for 18 months. Let us clear the air. Perhaps a vote would do it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes available to me this evening I should like to illustrate some ways in which the Canadian public has been very well served during the tenure of the last five Liberal ministers of finance, Messrs. Sharp, Benson, Turner, Macdonald, and the present day Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
During the period 1968 to 1977, personal disposable income per capita increased as much as 118 per cent. Real per capita disposable income rose 52 per cent, which was more than double the increase in the United States. During 1968 to 1978 the number of Canadians living below the poverty line was cut by half. From 1973 to 1976 the OECD reported that Canada had the third highest rate of growth in the western world. Further, the OECD reports that Canada's per capita income of $8,400 is third among major industrialized countries, and the United States was fourth. Each year during the 1970s Canada created more new jobs than any other major industrialized country. The increase averaged 3 per cent in Canada, 2 per cent in the United States, and less than 1 per cent in Japan and Europe. In 1978, ten million Canadians were working, whereas in 1968 7.5 million Canadians were working. From July, 1977, to July, 1978, 422,000 new jobs were created in the country.
Finally, I should like to refer to the opinions of a distinguished member of the Conservative party, the former treasurer of the province of Ontario, in terms of the economic policy of the opposition, wherein he said the following:
Former Ontario Treasurer Darcy McKeough emerged from six months of private life on the weekend to chastise federal Conservative leader Joseph Clark for suggesting the need for a larger deficit.-
The reference to the federal opposition leader was brief, but significant because it was made at a dinner in his honour before an audience that included Premier William Davis, several provincial cabinet ministers and many prominent Chatham-Kent Tories.
Let me further quote:
In an interview Mr. McKeough said he is alarmed with the federal Conservative party's stand on the deficit. It is nonsense to think that the tap can be turned on and just as quickly turned off-

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-RADIO AND TELEVISION SERVICES IN ENGLISH AND FRENCH
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-RADIO AND TELEVISION SERVICES IN ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) what he had done and what more he planned to do to hasten the full implementation of the CBC's so called accelerated coverage plan. The question I asked was prompted by a recommendation of the Task Force on Canadian Unity. As a matter of fact it was the first of the specific recommendations in the document entitled, "A Future Together". What the specific recommendation said was that the principles of equality, status, rights and privileges of the English and French languages for all purposes declared by the Parliament of Canada within its sphere of jurisdiction should be entrenched in the constitution.
Among the purposes referred to was No. 5, namely, the right of every person to have access to radio and television services in both the French and English languages. Allow me to show how the accelerated coverage plan, the ACP, is designed to meet the need and fulfil what this Liberal government already regards as the right of Canadians.
The ACP is a plan for accelerated extension of television and radio services in Canada. The terms of reference for the ACP are as follows: to provide CBC national service in the appropriate official language, English or French, to all unserved areas containing 500 or more people which can be covered by a single radio or television transmitter, and those points presently inadequately served and, secondly, to complete the implementation of the plan within a five year period from the date of approval.
Mr. Speaker, the memo which I have outlining the terms is dated December 3, 1974. Thus, by the end of this year the detailed plan for each region should be fully implemented. On this memo from the CBC there is written in alongside this term of reference a note which says "will be considerably more". That is to say, the time schedule of the CBC is not about to be met; the plan is not on target with respect to time. One could ask, what else is new? Governments and their agencies are rarely on time unless we have a crisis of some kind on our hands.
There is more to my complaint than that. This plan, which was to take five years to complete, was at the very beginning started with the CBC holding meetings with representatives of each region to ensure there was local and regional input. This was to be used in the development of the plan. From this work a detailed plan for each region took effect. Included among the topics discussed at these regional meetings was that of the priority of the projects within the five year time span. Frenchspeaking Canadians living in northwestern Ontario, where they constitute in many communities a majority of the population, or at least a significant percentage, were told their need for French language radio and television was of the highest priority and they would begin to enjoy this service at the very

January 29, 1979
Adjournment Debate
latest by the end of year three of the plan. That means they should have had the service by Christmas of 1977. There is some vague hope that it may come by Christmas of this year, but the degree of commitment by CBC to the accelerated coverage plan is very vague and uncertain.
I have the great privilege of representing in my constituency a great many Franco-Ontarians, and I hope in the future to represent many more as the boundaries of my constituency are pushed into north-eastern Ontario. Franco-Ontarians are a patient, tolerant, and good natured group of people who have contributed much to the economy of northern Ontario, particularly in the forest products industry, as entrepreneurs and as professional people. It has been a struggle for them, however, to maintain the use of their language in Ontario where there is but one official language, namely, English.
The province of Ontario has been rather slow in many cases to provide educational facilities and other services in the French language. Of course, the situation is improving, but Ontario at this time extends no statutory rights to the Frenchspeaking people of the province in terms of the right to use their language and to have services in that language.
Very recently a private members' bill to that effect was given second reading in the Ontario legislature. The premier made it clear, howewer, that there would be no way in which the bill would be brought forward for third reading and passed into law. The bill was not designed to make Ontario a bilingual province, but to give Franco-Ontarians service in their own language where there was a significant number and where there was a demand for the use of the French language.
Franco-Ontarians have learned to expect little from Queen's Park, but they do have high expectations of the federal government. There are federal agencies and departments which are bilingual in the main, but there is a strip of northern Ontario running from Sault Ste. Marie up to Nakina on the main line of the CNR where a significant number of French-speaking Canadians live, and they are still waiting for the CBC French language radio and television network they were promised. Some of these communities have a French-speaking population to the extent of 60 per cent or more. They believe that a promise was made and that there was a commitment, but the service they were told they would get is not yet there.
They are beginning to get a sense of impatience, and that is quite understandable. Recently an unlicensed service has done something to fill the void, but CBC must be instructed to meet their obligations. Additional funds were voted by parliament for the accelerated coverage plan. We know that it is an extensive plan and that there are many difficulties. However, my colleagues and myself have been frustrated in our efforts to speed up the implementation of the ACP. Therefore I would ask the Secretary of State to use his office to make it clear to the CBC that this plan is of the highest priority, and in the
name of national unity the CBC should step on the footfeed and get the accelerated coverage plan completed.
Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, I would commence by reiterating to the hon. member the words the minister used in a response to that question just a few days ago, that he shared the concerns of the hon. member and that, indeed, the hon. member has been tenacious in trying to ensure that in fact the schedule which was attached by the CBC to the ACP program would be adhered to if at all possible. In addition to that, the minister has made the increase he indicated he would make and, although they have been preliminary by way of response to date, the CBC has provided some information which I would gladly provide to the member this evening.
The CBC takes the position and relates that in fact the accelerated cover plan is designed to ensure that CBC radio and television service will be extended to all communities where 500 or more people are unserved or inadequately served in the appropriate language. The ACP is implemented under a strict formula system of priorities which takes into account such factors as population, capital and operating expenses, provincial equalization, and geographic and cultural isolation. Implementation is, in this way, as fair and equitable as it can be made. All communities identified for inclusion in the ACP are listed according to their priority under this formula, and "community" in this case also means minorities within a larger language group, such as the French-speaking population of Thunder Bay and the English-speaking population of Chicoutimi.
Provision of funds for the implementation of the ACP is made within the CBC's regular capital and operating budgets. As for the plan itself, it was originally to be completed in the period 1974 to 1979. A number of factors, however, have brought about a stretching out of that period by approximately three years. These factors include a sharp rise in costs, which are now approximately double the 1975 estimate, and the difficulty of finding enough qualified technical personnel for the installation of the more thr u 600 transmitters involved in the plan. Other factors were delays in the production by the electronic industry of the necessary equipment and budget constraints in 1978-79 and 1979-80.
I realize that this is not as complete an answer as the hon. member would require, Mr. Speaker, but it does give some kind of revised estimate in terms of the implementation time. It is something that both the minister and the hon. member would want to pursue when this matter comes before committee during steady of the estimates.
